A companion deep-dive to the main MABench evaluation,
[*Machines Improving Agents*](../the-benchmark/index.qmd). MABench hands an
optimization method a copy of a seed agent and a metered budget; the method
checkpoints whatever it thinks is its best, and only those checkpoints are
scored — later, on a **sealed** test split it never sees. Everything here is
the *frontier-worker slice* of the grid: worker `gpt-5.6-luna`, meta model
`gpt-5.6-sol` or `claude-opus-5`, with every lift measured as Δ over the
seed's own genesis. Keep the noise floor in mind — one full eval's
run-to-run spread is a few points, so a lift smaller than that is
indistinguishable from re-scoring an unchanged agent (the
[main post](../the-benchmark/index.qmd) reports the exact floor).

Meta-Harness reads the agent's failures and rewrites the harness around a
fixed worker. On the frontier-worker slice it is the grid's sample-efficiency
frontier: it reaches equal-or-better best-dev with 5–10× fewer candidates
than GEPA — sol's GPQA-medium run hit dev 0.905 in 34 candidates for \$42,
against GEPA's 197 candidates and \$59 for 0.891 — usually finds its winner
by half-budget, then plateaus. And unlike a prompt evolver, the surface it
edits is architectural, not textual.<!-- TODO: figure — MH vs GEPA
candidates-to-best-dev, and the τ² abstraction-vs-enumeration pair -->

**What it edits is structure.** On GPQA its winner threw out the one-call
solver and rebuilt the worker into a three-call blind ensemble with an
adjudicator told that "neither candidate is authoritative and agreement is
not evidence"; the prompt stayed tiny, and what it learned from the training
traces was distilled into failure-mode heuristics that carry no answers ("do
not assume an electric dipole when symmetry can cancel it"). On the very
cell where [GEPA memorized the train set](../gepa/index.qmd) and lost 4
points, Meta-Harness gained **+4.0** — same worker, same budget, opposite
outcome, because it changed the machine rather than the crib sheet.

**But whether that structure transfers hinges on one thing: does the
proposer abstract the failure, or transcribe it?** τ² gives the cleanest
natural experiment in the grid — the same method, the same ~3× prompt
growth, the same trace-mining loop, applied to two seeds, with opposite
results:

- *strong seed, +8.5 test:* the failures it read were compiled into
  domain-general invariants — "transaction recovery is part of completion…
  use fresh tool evidence, select the user's already-stated fallback"; "a
  rejected upgrade never cancels an authorized baggage change."
- *medium seed, −7.3 test:* the same kind of trace evidence was enumerated
  into scenario-shaped micro-patches keyed to named rollouts — "retail:104
  failed on several cross-order item actions", "airline:20 quoted a \$351
  upgrade but the mutation charged \$1,200" — hardening into rules pinned to
  the exact situations it had seen.

The two differ only in abstraction level, and **the dev split could not tell
them apart**: the winning candidate scored 0.6909 against a runner-up's
0.6848, well inside one standard error. Trace access is Meta-Harness's real
edge — it finds *causes* where a score-only method sees only directions —
and also its risk, because a cause can be written down as a general
mechanism or as a lookup keyed to the instance that produced it, and both
raise the dev number identically.

**And the diagnosis is not the binding constraint — the selector is.**
Roughly 80% of the proposer's proposals cite specific trace evidence:
explicit rollout ids, or quantified failure statistics like "verify fired on
56 traces and changed the answer zero times." Yet grounded proposals score
no better on dev than ungrounded ones — in three of four analyzed runs the
grounded mean is flat-to-slightly-lower. The method is already reading the
traces well. What it lacks is a selection signal that can tell an abstracted
fix from a transcribed one — exactly the gap the
[main evaluation](../the-benchmark/index.qmd) keeps hitting.

**Robustness is part of the result, not a footnote.** The two meta models
run the same method very differently. Opus reads like an investigator — 3.3
hours of proposer time on one GPQA cell, re-reading old rollouts and writing
throwaway Python to quantify a mechanism before touching a candidate — at
\$28.53 of meta spend, and on CharXiv more meta dollars than all the
evaluation combined. Sol runs the same loop in 18 minutes for \$5.10 by
bulk-dumping every candidate's source in one command — which is exactly what
killed it: that single giant exec crashed 7 of its 18 GPQA-strong proposer
sessions and aborted all three of its CharXiv runs outright, while opus
completed 40 of 40 on both tiers. Neither cost nor caution bought a
sealed-test gain that clears the noise — but a method×model pair that
crashes 40% of its sessions has a different expected value than its
completed-run mean advertises, and that failure rate belongs next to the Δ.

The one-line read: Meta-Harness is the most sample-efficient searcher in the
grid and the best diagnostician, rebuilding worker architecture from
correctly-read failures — and it still can't reliably bank a sealed-test
lift, because the dev signal it selects on cannot distinguish the invariant
it should keep from the instance-patch it should throw away.
